summary: Give the Deferred payment loan calculator the date of balance, the monthly payment, the loan term and the interest rate and it returns original monthly payment. Think of it as a shortcut for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. The panel waits for the button. Edit a field, press Calculate, and compare — one input at a time is enough to see what drives the answer.

sections.title: How does the Deferred payment loan calculator work?
sections.html:
The Deferred payment loan calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports original monthly payment in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the compounding frequency, the interest treatment and the payment frequency); then you give the date of balance and the deferment from; then you type in the monthly payment, the loan term, the interest rate and the fee.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

sections.title: The formula behind the Deferred payment loan calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Original monthly payment=(loan amount, payment frequency, loan term, M, interest rate, fee)
Original loan term=(loan amount, payment frequency, monthly payment, M, interest rate, fee)
Payoff date without=((((estimation based on..., loan amount, interest treatment, date of balance, deferment from, payments deferred for..., M, interest rate, loan term, monthly payment, repayment by...))))
Payoff date with=((((estimation based on..., loan amount, interest treatment, date of balance, deferment from, payments deferred for..., M, interest rate, loan term, monthly payment, repayment by...))))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Time, opening in years / months
  • %, opening in percent
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Time, opening in years / months
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Deferred payment loan calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Sizing up a purchase before you commit to it
  • Comparing two offers that quote their costs in different ways
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the date of balance, the monthly payment and the loan term — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Dates are compared date to date in your own time zone, so a daylight-saving change will not shift the count by a day.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Deferred payment loan calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns original monthly payment, derived from the date of balance, the monthly payment and the loan term. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Deferred payment loan calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the date of balance, the monthly payment, the loan term and the interest rate, which is 21 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter loan amount in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Loan amount opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (5 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports M = 0. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Deferred payment loan calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
